skip_reason: Inbound rescheduling call on an already-booked move, not new business. A third-party coordinator (Nina) called to move an existing booking for her client off Tuesday the 22nd; Chris looked up the existing job, confirmed Monday the 21st availability, and re-set the afternoon window. The only estimate talk was trimming an already-quoted job ('I don't think it's gonna be the six hours, I was just being overly cautious') - no prospecting, no pricing pitch, no booking attempt. The sales rubric does not apply.
top_strength: Handled a reschedule cleanly and did not just take the date change at face value - he re-opened the inventory to protect estimate accuracy: "Is there any way we can get a more like, in-depth inventory list just to make sure nothing's missed." He then walked beds, night stands, coffee table and dining set one by one and revised six hours back down, which is exactly the behavior the estimate-accuracy work is chasing.
coaching_note: He burned about a third of a short call hunting for the booking ("I'm sorry, I'm having trouble finding the booking on Tuesday. What was that clients name again") because he searched the caller's name first on a third-party-coordinated move. On agent/coordinator calls, ask up front whose name the job is under. Also worth noting: he revised the estimate down verbally but never restated the new hour count or dollar figure to the caller before ending - she hung up without a number.
phone_presence_notes: Polite and efficient with a warm close ("Yeah, you're very welcome"), but largely transactional - repeated "let me check" dead air during the booking search and no acknowledgment of the caller's scheduling bind for her client.
